title: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Sequential Data Processing and Learning Temporal Dependencies · Subject: Neural Network Architectures. Exact question texts, seven unique diagrams and beginner-first explanations with optional depth.
hero:
RECURRENT NEURAL NETWORK · ILLUSTRATED OVERVIEW

An RNN reads new information while carrying forward its memory.

The changing hidden state is a learned summary, not a word-for-word storage system. Recurrent parameters are shared across all time steps.

questions.stem: What is a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), and how does it differ from a traditional Feedforward Neural Network when processing sequential information such as text, speech, or time-series data?
options: A feedforward network naturally remembers previous inputs, while an RNN processes all tokens independently.
An RNN reuses a hidden state across time, while feedforward layers lack that recurrent memory.
An RNN reads all words simultaneously without carrying information between its separate time steps.
A feedforward network updates the same hidden state after each word, unlike any recurrent model.
questions.explanation: In simple words: An RNN reads a sequence in order and carries a changing memory forward. A regular feedforward network does not pass that memory between steps.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: An RNN consumes ordered vectors x₁,x₂,…,x_T. A recurrent cell combines the newest input xₜ with hidden state hₜ₋₁ and produces hₜ, which can inform the next step. Feedforward networks do not have this built-in recurrence, though they can be applied across multiple positions as independent functions. The cell parameters are shared over time, unlike a new set of weights for each word. This supports text, speech and time series but creates sequential dependencies during computation.
questions.figure:
01 · Basic architecture

A recurrent cell receives memory from the previous time step

Feedforward layers do not inherently carry a sequence state; the simple RNN does. Both can be parts of larger architectures.

questions.stem: What is the Hidden State in an RNN, and how does it act as a form of memory that carries information from previous time steps to help the network understand the current input?
options: The hidden state is a saved training label that never changes as new inputs arrive.
The hidden state stores every earlier token perfectly, without any chance of losing information.
The hidden state is a model weight that changes only when training finishes an epoch.
The hidden state summarizes earlier inputs and updates as the network reads each new step.
questions.explanation: In simple words: The hidden state is the network's running summary. Each new input updates it, so earlier information can affect the next decision.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Hidden state hₜ is a fixed-width learned vector representing useful information from the sequence prefix. A simple update is hₜ=tanh(Wₓxₜ+Wₕhₜ₋₁+b). Its meaning is learned from the objective; it is not a cache containing the original words. The latest input can change or overwrite previous information, and basic RNNs often struggle to retain distant details across many steps.
questions.figure:
02 · What memory means

New inputs update a limited hidden-state summary

The words inside the capsules are teaching metaphors. Real states are vectors of learned numbers, not explicit text labels.

questions.stem: Imagine an RNN reading the sentence "The dog chased the ball." How does it process each word one at a time, update its Hidden State, and use information from earlier words to understand the sentence or predict what comes next?
options: It reads words in order, updating hidden state so earlier words can influence later predictions.
It encodes every word separately, discarding all earlier context before choosing the next word.
It reads the sentence backward only, because recurrent networks cannot process normal word order.
It stores all words unchanged in a fixed dictionary instead of updating a hidden state.
questions.explanation: In simple words: The RNN reads “The,” then “dog,” then “chased,” and so on. Its changing memory helps later words connect with earlier ones.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Starting with an initial state h₀, often zero, the model processes the vector for “The” and computes h₁. It then combines “dog” with h₁ to produce h₂, “chased” with h₂ to produce h₃, and continues through “the” and “ball.” Each state is based on the previous words and current word. An optional output head can make a prediction at each position or after the final token. Subject and action cues are intuitive examples, not guaranteed explicit fields in the hidden vector.
questions.figure:
03 · Step-by-step sentence reading

Each new word changes the memory used for later words

An RNN can learn relationships among subject, action and object, but it may lose details as a sequence gets longer.

questions.stem: How does an RNN mathematically calculate its Hidden State and output at each time step using input vectors, recurrent weight matrices, bias terms, and activation functions, and how are the same parameters reused across the sequence?
options: Each word gets different recurrent weights, so the model learns a different network for positions.
The recurrence simply adds token indices directly without matrix multiplications or nonlinear activation functions.
The same matrices combine current input and previous hidden state, then an activation updates memory.
The hidden state uses only the current word; earlier states never enter the calculation.
questions.explanation: In simple words: At every time step, the RNN combines the new input and previous memory using the same learned weights, then updates its state.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: For a tanh Elman RNN, hₜ=tanh(Wₓxₜ+Wₕhₜ₋₁+bₕ). An optional output projection is yₜ=Wᵧhₜ+bᵧ. If xₜ has width d_in and hₜ has width d_h, Wₓ has shape [d_h,d_in], Wₕ shape [d_h,d_h], and the same matrices and biases are reused at all T positions. In PyTorch, nn.RNN(4,5,batch_first=True) takes [batch,time,4], returns sequence outputs [batch,time,5] and a final state [num_layers,batch,5] for a unidirectional model. Actual output mapping varies with the prediction task.
questions.figure:
04 · RNN equations

The current input and previous hidden state use shared learned matrices

This illustrates a basic tanh RNN. The output projection depends on the task, and PyTorch uses transposed internal matrix orientation.

questions.stem: How are RNNs trained using Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT), and why can repeatedly propagating gradients across long sequences cause Vanishing and Exploding Gradient problems that make learning long-term dependencies difficult?
options: BPTT changes weights after every word without computing derivatives through any earlier time steps.
BPTT unfolds recurrent steps and sends gradients backward; repeated products can shrink or grow.
BPTT avoids long gradient chains completely, so recurrent models never face unstable gradients.
BPTT calculates only output gradients and ignores the reused recurrent parameters during training.
questions.explanation: In simple words: BPTT follows the sequence backward to calculate learning signals. Over many steps, those signals may shrink too much or grow too large.
questions.technicalExplanation:
Detailed explanation: Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) unfolds the recurrent computation across time steps and differentiates loss backward through the reused cell. Early gradients contain repeated recurrent Jacobian products; they may shrink (vanishing gradients) or grow (exploding gradients). Gradient clipping limits large gradients, truncated BPTT reduces how far back each training segment differentiates, and gated cells often improve long-range learning. This self-contained PyTorch example was executed on CPU 2.10, showing sequence outputs, final state, a finite recurrent gradient and stacked-bidirectional shapes:
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(11)
rnn = nn.RNN(input_size=4, hidden_size=5, batch_first=True)
x = torch.randn(2, 4, 4)  # batch, time, features
outputs, last_hidden = rnn(x)
outputs.mean().backward()  # backpropagation through time
print(tuple(outputs.shape))       # (2, 4, 5)
print(tuple(last_hidden.shape))   # (1, 2, 5)
print(torch.isfinite(rnn.weight_hh_l0.grad).all().item()) # True

bi = nn.RNN(4, 5, num_layers=2,
            bidirectional=True, batch_first=True)
bi_out, bi_hidden = bi(x)
print(tuple(bi_out.shape))     # (2, 4, 10)
print(tuple(bi_hidden.shape))  # (4, 2, 5)
Clipping does not by itself prevent vanishing gradients; and truncation can lose distant dependencies.
questions.figure:
05 · Why gradients can fail

Backpropagating through many time steps can shrink or amplify gradients

The curves are conceptual, not measured results. Long chains of derivatives cause the training difficulty; clipping addresses explosions.

questions.stem: How do Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) overcome limitations of traditional RNNs through gating mechanisms, and how do their architectures differ in controlling information retention, forgetting, and hidden-state updates?
options: LSTMs manage cell and hidden states with gates; GRUs use simpler gating and one state.
LSTMs and GRUs remove recurrence entirely, so neither can carry useful information between separate time steps.
LSTMs keep just one gate, while GRUs require separate cell memory with four gates.
LSTMs can preserve every past token without errors, while GRUs permanently forget past words.
questions.explanation: In simple words: LSTMs use gates and a separate cell memory to control information flow. GRUs use fewer gates and a simpler hidden-state update.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: LSTM computes separate hidden state hₜ and cell state cₜ. Forget, input, and output gates regulate their flow: cₜ=fₜ⊙cₜ₋₁+iₜ⊙gₜ and hₜ=oₜ⊙tanh(cₜ). GRUs use a single hidden state with an update gate and a reset gate affecting a candidate. This can reduce parameter count compared with an otherwise similarly sized LSTM, though implementations vary. Gates can help retain useful information and support gradients across more time steps, but neither architecture guarantees perfect long-range memory or universally faster inference.
questions.figure:
06 · LSTM versus GRU

LSTM manages a separate cell state; GRU uses simpler gates

LSTM has forget, input and output gates; GRU uses update and reset gates. Their exact speed and quality depend on the task.

questions.stem: How do Bidirectional RNNs, Stacked RNNs, and Sequence-to-Sequence Encoder-Decoder architectures handle complex sequential tasks, and how do RNN-based models compare with Transformers in terms of parallelization, long-range dependencies, computational complexity, inference latency, and real-world deployment?
options: Bidirectional RNNs only read forward, stacked RNNs eliminate state, and Transformers require sequential training.
Stacked RNNs process only one time step, while encoder–decoders prohibit variable output lengths.
Transformers cannot handle long-range relationships, while recurrent networks always parallelize every time step.
Bidirectional RNNs read both directions; stacked layers add depth; encoder–decoders map sequences.
questions.explanation: In simple words: Bidirectional RNNs read both ways; stacked RNNs add layers; encoder–decoders transform sequences. Transformers can process training positions more simultaneously.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Bidirectional RNNs run forward and backward over a complete sequence, combining features at each position; the reverse side needs future tokens, which is unsuitable for strictly online causal predictions. Stacked RNNs run multiple recurrent layers, where later layers read earlier layers' outputs. Sequence-to-sequence RNN encoder–decoders process a source sequence and generate a target, often aided by attention. The recurrence chain uses O(T) time steps for fixed hidden width and does not fully parallelize across time, while full Transformer self-attention performs O(T²) pair comparisons but parallelizes many positions during training. Practical device latency, memory, model width, batching, kernel support and KV caching determine performance. RNNs can suit streaming and compact deployment; Transformers can excel on large-scale contextual tasks.
questions.figure:
07 · Architecture trade-offs

RNN variants add context or depth; Transformers parallelize sequence training

Bidirectional models need future context, so they are not directly causal. Actual performance depends on workload, hardware, sequence length and caching.
